knitr::opts_chunk$set(

has_shazam <- requireNamespace("shazam", quietly = TRUE)
imgt_dir <- path.expand(Sys.getenv("SIRUP_IMGT_DIR"))
has_imgt <- nzchar(imgt_dir) && dir.exists(imgt_dir) && has_shazam

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  **Time:** ~20 minutes.<br>
  **Data:** a saved SIRUP object of the example MG thymus data, plus its polygon file.<br>
  **Needs:** SIRUP, scoper, dowser, shazam, and the IMGT reference sequences for the germline and tree steps.
</div>

Here, we will work with the clones in a SIRUP object, build lineage trees for some of them, and pair each tree with the tissue.

A *clone* is a group of B or T cells that descend from one ancestor cell and share its receptor rearrangement. A *lineage tree* shows how the sequences of one clone relate to each other, where each tip is one sequence.
Pairing a tree with the tissue shows where each tip sits. At the end, we will compare distances in the tree with distances on the tissue.

SIRUP does not reimplement clone calling or tree building. It runs the Immcantation tools (scoper, dowser, shazam) on the receptor table inside the SIRUP object, then adds the spatial part: clone maps, trees paired with
tissue plots, and distances between tips in and between regions.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  This page starts with a saved SIRUP object, which is loaded below. To learn how the object is built, see `vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")`. To learn about the polygons used here, see `vignette("regions", package = "SIRUP")`.
</div>

## Load the example object

This code downloads a saved SIRUP object for MG thymus section 2, which is not part of the SIRUP package, and the polygon file for the section. Change `dest` to a folder you want to keep.
The function skips files that are already there. To see how the object was built, see `vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")`.

```{r download-data}
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = c(
    "mg_thymus_slice2.sirup.rds",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv"
  )
)
```

```{r libraries, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r setup}
sirup <- readSIRUP(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2.sirup.rds"))
sirup
```

The object holds two receptor slots, `"BCR"` and `"TCR"`, and the functions on this page read one slot at a time. This page works mostly on the BCR slot, so each call that reads
receptors has `slot = "BCR"`.

In this object, the comma in each `sequence_id` is replaced with `_`. dowser writes trees in Newick format, where a comma separates tips, so dowser renames tips that contain a comma.
With the comma gone, the tip names match the receptor table and SIRUP can find each tip on the tissue.

Each polygon in the example polygon file outlines one ectopic germinal center (eGC), a site in the thymus where B cells proliferate and mutate their receptors. Add the polygons to the
object with `addPolygons()`:

```{r add-polygons}
sirup <- addPolygons(
  sirup,
  polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
)
```

## Look at the clones

A clone is a group of receptors that descend from one ancestor cell. The BCR clones in this object were called with `scoper::hierarchicalClones()` through `updateReceptors()`, as shown in
`vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")`.

```{r clones, message = FALSE}
sirup
dplyr::n_distinct(getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR")$clone_id)
```

`hierarchicalClones()` groups sequences with the same V gene, J gene, and junction length, then joins sequences whose junctions differ by less than `threshold`. The SIRUP paper used
`threshold = 0.1` for BCRs. The function writes a `clone_id` column, which `updateReceptors()` records as the clone field. If a function writes a different column, record it with
`receptor_fields = list(clone = "my_clone_column")`.

TCRs do not mutate, so TCR clones are called with `scoper::identicalClones()`. This call runs it on the TCR slot:

```{r call-tcr-clones, message = FALSE}
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::identicalClones,
  slot = "TCR",
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
dplyr::n_distinct(getReceptors(sirup, slot = "TCR")$clone_id)
```

## Reconstruct germlines

The germline of a clone is the sequence of its unmutated ancestor, and a lineage tree starts at this sequence. `dowser::createGermlines()` reconstructs one germline for each clone from the IMGT reference sequences.
IMGT is the international database of immune receptor genes. The SIRUP paper made the germlines in the object and removed likely PCR chimeras.

SIRUP does not include the IMGT references. Download them, e.g., with the Immcantation script `fetch_imgtdb.sh`, and set the environment variable `SIRUP_IMGT_DIR` to the folder that holds the human V, D, and J FASTA
files, such as `~/share/germlines/imgt/human/vdj`. The germline and tree chunks on this page run only when that folder exists.

```{r germlines, eval = has_imgt, message = FALSE}
references <- dowser::readIMGT(imgt_dir)

sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  dowser::createGermlines,
  slot = "BCR",
  references = references,
  id = "sequence_id",
  nproc = 1
)

sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR", function(receptors) {
  chimera <- shazam::slideWindowDb(
    receptors,
    sequenceColumn = "sequence_alignment",
    germlineColumn = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
    mutThresh = 6,
    windowSize = 10
  )
  receptors[!chimera, ]
})
```

## Measure somatic hypermutation

Somatic hypermutation (SHM) is the process that introduces point mutations into B cell receptor genes. Use `shazam::observedMutations()` to count the mutations of each sequence against a germline. With clonal germlines, use
`germline_alignment_d_mask`. The chunk below uses `germline_alignment`, the germline that IgBLAST wrote for each sequence, so it runs without the IMGT references. The result goes in `mu_freq`, the fraction of mutated positions.

```{r shm, eval = has_shazam}
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  shazam::observedMutations,
  slot = "BCR",
  sequenceColumn = "sequence_alignment",
  germlineColumn = "germline_alignment",
  frequency = TRUE,
  combine = TRUE
)
summary(getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR")$mu_freq)
```

`plotReceptors()` can color spots by a numeric receptor column. Give the column to `value`. If a spot has several receptors, `value_combine` sets how SIRUP combines them, and the default is the mean.

```{r shm-map, eval = has_shazam}
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  group = "locus",
  value = "mu_freq",
  value_colors = c("white", "darkred"),
  receptor_size = 1.3,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  title = "Mean SHM frequency per spot"
)
```

## Choose clones to build trees for

Trees are most useful for expanded clones. The code below keeps clones that have 10 to 60 sequences and at least one sequence in an eGC, then sorts them by the number of sequences in eGCs.

```{r choose-clones}
clone_sizes <- getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR") %>%
  group_by(clone_id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_sequences = n(),
    n_in_gc = sum(!is.na(polygon_id)),
    n_gcs = n_distinct(na.omit(polygon_id)),
    gcs = paste(sort(unique(na.omit(polygon_id))), collapse = ", ")
  ) %>%
  filter(n_sequences >= 10, n_sequences <= 60, n_in_gc > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_in_gc))

head(clone_sizes)
tree_clones <- head(clone_sizes$clone_id, 3)
```

Plot the spots of the three chosen clones:

```{r clone-map}
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  group = "clone_id",
  group_val = tree_clones,
  receptor_size = 1.6,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  zoom = TRUE,
  title = "Selected clones"
)
```

## Build trees

Two functions run dowser on the object. `formatSpatialClones()` runs `dowser::formatClones()` and stores the result as an analysis. `getSpatialTrees()` runs `dowser::getTrees()` on a stored formatted-clone analysis and
stores the trees as another analysis. Both functions take the dowser arguments.

Tree building takes time for large clones, so first make a smaller object with only the clones of interest. `updateReceptors()` with `dplyr::filter()` does this.

```{r build-trees, eval = has_trees}
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, clone_id %in% tree_clones, slot = "BCR")

tree_sirup <- formatSpatialClones(
  tree_sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  analysis_name = "formatted_clones",
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = c("barcode_10x", "polygon_id")
)

set.seed(1)
tree_sirup <- getSpatialTrees(
  tree_sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  f_clones_analysis = "formatted_clones",
  analysis_name = "trees",
  build = "pratchet"
)

trees <- getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees")
trees
```

`traits` keeps the columns that the tree plots need. Keep the spatial ID, so SIRUP can put each tip on the tissue, and add any column to color by.

`build = "pratchet"` builds maximum parsimony trees, which is fast. The SIRUP paper used maximum likelihood (`build = "pml"`). For B cell models, use IgPhyML (`build = "igphyml"` with the `igphyml` path).

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  By default, `formatClones()` merges identical sequences into one tip, so a tip can stand for several sequences.
</div>

Store the trees in the main object:

```{r store-trees, eval = has_trees}
sirup <- setAnalysis(sirup, "trees", trees)
```

## Pair each tree with the tissue

`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` makes two plots for each clone: the lineage tree and a tissue map. Each tip has one color in both plots, so a tip of the tree can be found on the tissue.

```{r tree-pairs, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  trees,
  object = sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  clone_val = tree_clones,
  id = "sequence_id",
  zoom = TRUE,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black"
)
names(pairs)

pairs[[1]]
```

The result is a list with one element for each clone. Printing an element shows the tree and the map side by side. Each element also holds the `tree` plot and the `spatial_clone` plot, which can be used for a custom layout. Tips with a spot in this section are circles. Tips without a spot, such as bulk sequences, are squares and appear
in the tree only. Sequences in the same spot share a point on the map.

### Color tips by group

A clone with many tips is hard to read when each tip has its own color. `clusterTreesTips()` cuts each tree into `k` connected groups of related tips. The code below uses `k = 4` for every tree.

```{r tree-clusters, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 5.5}
clustered <- clusterTreesTips(
  trees,
  k = 4,
  id = "sequence_id",
  cluster = "tree_cluster"
)

cluster_pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  clustered,
  object = sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  clone_val = tree_clones,
  id = "sequence_id",
  color_by = "tree_cluster",
  zoom = TRUE,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  show_spatial_legend = TRUE
)

cluster_pairs[[1]]
```

With `k = "auto"`, the function chooses `k` for each tree from `k_range`. It stops when one more cut reduces the mean within-group patristic distance by less than `improvement_threshold`, which is 10% by default. A tree with
little structure can get `k = 1`, which gives all its tips one color.

`color_by` accepts any column of the dowser clone data. For example, `color_by = "polygon_id"` colors each tip by its eGC, because the code kept `polygon_id` in `traits`.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Tip</b> </p>
  `spatialCloneTreePairsToPDF(cluster_pairs, "tree_pairs.pdf", width = 12, height = 6)` writes one page for each clone.
</div>

## Compare tree distance with physical distance

Do sequences in the same eGC have shorter tree distances than sequences in different eGCs? The patristic distance between two tips is the sum of the branch lengths between them. `tipPatristicMatrix()` gives these distances
for a set of tips.

The code below takes the selected clone that spans the most eGCs and compares the tip pairs in the same eGC with the tip pairs in different eGCs.

```{r patristic, eval = has_trees}
multi_gc_clone <- clone_sizes %>%
  filter(clone_id %in% tree_clones) %>%
  slice_max(n_gcs, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  pull(clone_id)
multi_gc_clone

index <- which(trees$clone_id == multi_gc_clone)
clone_data <- trees$data[[index]]@data
tree <- trees$trees[[index]]

gc_tips <- clone_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(polygon_id), sequence_id %in% tree$tip.label) %>%
  select(sequence_id, polygon_id)

distances <- tipPatristicMatrix(tree, gc_tips$sequence_id)

pairs_table <- as.data.frame(as.table(distances)) %>%
  rename(tip_a = Var1, tip_b = Var2, distance = Freq) %>%
  filter(as.character(tip_a) < as.character(tip_b)) %>%
  mutate(
    gc_a = gc_tips$polygon_id[match(tip_a, gc_tips$sequence_id)],
    gc_b = gc_tips$polygon_id[match(tip_b, gc_tips$sequence_id)],
    pair = if_else(gc_a == gc_b, "same eGC", "different eGCs")
  )

pairs_table %>%
  group_by(pair) %>%
  summarise(n_pairs = n(), median_distance = median(distance))
```

The table gives the two medians. One clone cannot support a conclusion, because tip pairs share branches. The SIRUP paper ran this comparison over all eGC clones, with a mixed model that had a random effect for each clone.
